Inward
IN-wurd
adj. and adv. (interior, of the hidden man; rendering Hebrew tuchoth, qereb, Greek eso, esothen)
Old English inweard. Scripture's inward parts are not merely the anatomy but the seat of thought, will, and affection — the place where a man is what he is when no one is looking.

Biblical Definition

Inward in Scripture names the region God cares about most and man can see least. David states the requirement after his adultery: “Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom” (Psalm 51:6). The demand and the promise are joined — God requires truth where a man cannot manufacture it, and undertakes to teach wisdom there Himself. The principle is stated to Samuel at the anointing of David, and it corrects a prophet: “the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). Paul then uses the inward man for the regenerate self in two of the most honest sentences in his writings. In Romans 7 it is the seat of a genuine delight that his members contradict: “I delight in the law of God after the inward man” (Romans 7:22). In 2 Corinthians it is the part of him that is going the opposite direction from his body: “though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Two processes run at once in every Christian — a visible decay and an invisible renewal — and only one of them will be reported by a mirror.

Webster 1828 Definition

The hidden man. God desires truth in the inward parts and looks on the heart where man looks on the outward appearance; Paul delights in God's law after the inward man, and reports that it is renewed daily while the outward man perishes.

expand to see more

INWARD, a. [Sax. inweard.] Internal; interior; placed or being within.

2. Intimate; domestic; familiar.

3. Seated in the mind or soul; as inward joy or grief.

INWARD, adv. Toward the inside; as, to bend a thing inward.

INWARDS, n. plu. The bowels; the intestines; and figuratively, the seat of the affections. Truth in the inward parts. Ps. 51.

Key Scripture

Psalm 51:6 — "Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom."

1 Samuel 16:7 — "But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."

Romans 7:22 — "For I delight in the law of God after the inward man:"

2 Corinthians 4:16 — "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day."

Modern Corruption

The biblical inwardness — a heart God searches, requires truth in, and renews — has been replaced by an inwardness that is self-authenticating, in which the inner life is consulted as an oracle rather than examined as a defendant.

expand to see more

Modern spirituality is intensely inward and almost never self-suspecting. It looks in to find the true self, the authentic desire, the inner voice, and it treats what it finds as evidence. Psalm 51 goes inward in the opposite spirit: David asks God to look, because he cannot trust his own report, and the psalm ends by asking for a clean heart to be created rather than uncovered. Jeremiah 17:9-10 states the same logic — the heart is deceitful and unsearchable by its owner, and the LORD searches it. The difference is not in the direction of attention but in who is authorised to give the verdict. An inwardness that consults itself will always ratify itself; an inwardness that submits to being searched can actually be changed.

The opposite corruption is the outward religion that 1 Samuel 16:7 was spoken against, and it survives everywhere. Churches still weigh countenance and stature — presence, articulacy, success, the family that photographs well — and Samuel, a genuine prophet, was doing it in that very verse until God stopped him. What Scripture puts in place of appearance is not indifference to the visible but a different order of evidence: fruit over time, faithfulness in what is least, conduct in the household, and reputation among outsiders, all of which are slow and none of which impress at first sight. Paul's 2 Corinthians 4:16 is the pastoral pay-off. A man whose worth is located in the outward man is on a losing schedule, since the outward man is perishing on a fixed timetable; a man being renewed inwardly gets better as he gets worse.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tuchoth (the inward parts, from a root meaning to overlay or coat) and qereb (the midst, inner part); Greek eso (within) and esothen (from within), with ho eso anthropos, the inward man.

expand to see more

Hebrew tuchoth (H2910) — the inward parts; a rare word, used in Psalm 51:6 and Job 38:36.

Hebrew qereb (H7130) — the midst, inward part; used of the new spirit put within in Ezekiel 36:26-27.

Hebrew lebab (H3824) — heart, inner man; what the LORD looks on in 1 Samuel 16:7.

Greek eso (G2080) — within, inner; in the phrase ho eso anthropos, the inward man (Romans 7:22; 2 Corinthians 4:16; Ephesians 3:16).

Greek anakainoo (G341) — to renew, make new again; the verb in 2 Corinthians 4:16, in the present passive: is being renewed.

Usage

"“Thou desirest truth in the inward parts” — required where a man cannot manufacture it, and given by the God who requires it."

"“Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” — spoken to correct a prophet in the act."

"“The inward man is renewed day by day” — two processes at once, and only one shows in a mirror."
